reader.title: Caldwell depositors' seizure of J. S. Danford
bases: Depositors of a failed Caldwell, Kansas, bank took banker J. S. Danford and cashier Smith from officers and held them under open threats of hanging unless the money was paid, a threatened lynching that ended without a killing (A2, A12, A18).

No one was killed: Danford and Smith were held by an armed crowd of depositors acting without legal authority on the claim that the banker had swindled them, but both were released after a settlement (A12, A14, A16).
Separate dispatches from Wellington, Hunnewell and Caldwell, a Kansas weekly and Danford's own interview agree that depositors took him from officers and threatened his life (A2, A4, A6, A12, A18).

summary.text: The Caldwell depositors' seizure of J. S. Danford was the capture and detention of the owner of failed banks at Caldwell and Hunnewell, Kansas, and his cashier, Smith, by angry depositors in late November and early December 1881.
Taken from officers at Wellington, the two men were held at Caldwell under open threats that Danford would be hanged unless he paid the depositors.
No one was killed, and Danford was released after a compromise about December 5; papers across the country reported the affair as a lynching threat and a frontier way of settling a bank failure.
Danford, who lived at Osage City, ran banks in Osage County and a second pair at Caldwell and Hunnewell in Sumner County.
According to the Emporia Weekly News, the money ran out on Friday, November 25, when a depositor held a pistol to Cashier Smith's head and demanded his deposit.

Depositors were further angered by reports that the Caldwell bank's collateral and books had been taken to Newton while deposits were still being received, and that Danford had assigned his real estate to Col. Hood of Emporia.
Danford and Smith left by freight train for Wichita, where officers arrested them and brought them back to Wellington.

An armed body of men from Caldwell then arrived at Wellington, and in Danford's own later account a mob of 200 took the two from the sheriff, put revolvers to their heads and brought them to Caldwell on a special train.
A Wellington dispatch of November 29 reported that the men were under heavy guard day and night and that Sheriff Thralls said he could do nothing against the mob.
At Caldwell the crowd demanded "the money or his life," while armed men from Hunnewell waited to take Danford in turn.
Tanner and Denman, men suspected of helping move the collateral, were found hidden in a livery stable at Wellington and made to talk under threat.
A Hunnewell dispatch of December 1 said it was claimed in the streets that Danford would be "strung up, but not killed," and that any militia sent to rescue him would be disbanded.
By the Sun's Caldwell report of December 3, the rope had been put around Danford's neck three times, and a party from Hunnewell had ridden through town with revolvers and Winchesters.
A heavy depositor, Mr. Cosine, told the crowd that lynching Danford would leave them with ten cents on the dollar, and the mob dispersed, leaving him under a guard of three in a hotel.
Danford later described a preacher reading him a funeral sermon while a wagon stood at the door and armed men stood around the room.
A committee of seven depositors took over negotiations, and Smith was paroled to go to Emporia to look for collateral, returning as he had promised.

A Caldwell dispatch of December 5 reported Danford released on security for half the depositors' claims, while the Chicago Tribune gave the terms as 50 cents on the dollar in cash and the rest within a year, secured by real estate.
No arrest or prosecution of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.
The story moved by wire from Wellington, Hunnewell and Caldwell into papers from Maine to Utah between November 29 and mid-December.

Wire items called the bankers "swindlers" and "defaulters" and the crowd "exasperated depositors," and headlines such as "Must Pay Up or Die," "The Kansas Method" and "Workings of the Kansas Plan" treated the threats as a regional method of debt collection.
The Emporia Weekly News, close to Danford's home, played down the lynching talk and expected him to pay in full.

The Chicago Tribune printed Danford's own account from a Kansas City Journal letter under a mocking headline that called him "The Mob-Manled [Mauled] Banker" and "the Mulberry Sellers of Kansas bankers."
No article gives the race of anyone involved, and none frames the affair in racial terms.
Copies of the same Hunnewell dispatch disagree on figures, giving the Caldwell deposits as about $50,000 or "$ 1,000" and Danford's offer to his guards as $10,000 or $1,000 each.
A Maysville brief instead said Danford had "disgorged thirty thousand dollars" under threats of death.

accounts.label: Wire dispatches from Wellington and Hunnewell
accounts.gist: Depositors held Danford and Smith under heavy guard and openly threatened that Danford must settle or die; the sheriff said he was powerless.

accounts.label: Caldwell dispatches
accounts.gist: The crowd demanded 'the money or his life'; a rope was put around Danford's neck three times, but heavy depositors argued him down and a committee took over negotiations.

accounts.label: Emporia Weekly News
accounts.gist: Reported the arrest and the armed party from Caldwell but expected that 'better councils' would prevent a lynching.

accounts.label: Danford's own account
accounts.gist: A mob of 200 took him and Smith from the sheriff at Wellington, put revolvers to their heads, brought them to Caldwell by special train and kept them under threat, including a mock funeral sermon.

framing.detail: Wire items called the bankers 'swindlers' and 'defaulters' and the crowd 'exasperated depositors', reporting the threats without condemnation.
Headlines such as 'Must Pay Up or Die', 'The Kansas Method' and 'Workings of the Kansas Plan' presented the seizure as a regional way of settling a bank failure.
The Emporia Weekly News, near Danford's base, played down the lynching talk and predicted he would pay every cent.
The Chicago Tribune ran Danford's own story under 'The Mob-Manled [Mauled] Banker of Kansas Wugs [Wags] His Tongue—A Racy Yarn', mocking him as 'the Mulberry Sellers of Kansas bankers'.
